mcqs.question: A company's employees all browse the internet through one gateway box; external websites see requests coming from that box's IP, not each employee's laptop. Which type of proxy is this gateway?
options: A reverse proxy, because it reverses the direction of the connection
An API gateway, because it manages employee identities
A forward proxy, because it hides the client (each employee) from the server they're contacting
A load balancer, because it's spreading employee requests across servers
mcqs.explanation: Hiding the requester's identity from whatever they're contacting is the forward-proxy pattern by definition. It isn't reversing any direction — a reverse proxy hides the server side instead — managing identity isn't what makes something a gateway here, and there's no indication of multiple destination servers being balanced across.

mcqs.question: A backend fleet has no TLS certificates installed on any server, yet clients connect over HTTPS successfully. What is most likely handling this?
options: Each backend server is silently generating its own certificate on the fly
The client's browser is falling back to plain HTTP without telling the user
A forward proxy is decrypting the traffic before it reaches the client
A reverse proxy is terminating TLS and forwarding plain HTTP to backends over a trusted internal network
mcqs.explanation: TLS termination at the reverse proxy is exactly this pattern — the proxy holds the certificate, decrypts once, and talks plain HTTP internally. Servers don't spontaneously generate valid certificates, browsers wouldn't silently drop an HTTPS connection to plain HTTP without warning, and a forward proxy sits on the client's side of the conversation, not positioned to do this.

mcqs.question: You're building a service mesh where hundreds of microservices need traffic policy that can change without restarting anything, driven by a central control plane. Which of the three proxies is built specifically around this use case?
options: Envoy, via its dynamic configuration APIs (xDS)
NGINX, via its static configuration file reloads
HAProxy, via its connection-throughput optimizations
None of the three — service meshes require custom-built proxies
mcqs.explanation: Envoy's xDS APIs are specifically designed for a control plane to push configuration changes to many proxies live, exactly the service-mesh requirement described. NGINX's traditional model favors config-file reloads, HAProxy's strength lies elsewhere (raw throughput), and popular service meshes like Istio are built on Envoy rather than needing bespoke proxies.

mcqs.question: A team says "our load balancer and reverse proxy are the same NGINX instance, so the two terms mean the same thing." What's the flaw in that reasoning?
options: NGINX cannot actually perform load balancing, only reverse proxying

The two responsibilities often run on the same instance, but they're still separable — a pure L4 load balancer with no caching or TLS termination, or a caching reverse proxy with a single backend, are both real examples that don't overlap
Load balancing and reverse proxying are unrelated concepts that never appear together in practice
A reverse proxy is just an older, deprecated name for what's now called a load balancer
mcqs.explanation: NGINX absolutely can load balance (ruling out A), the two concepts do frequently co-occur in the same instance (ruling out C), and reverse proxy isn't a deprecated synonym for load balancer (ruling out D) — it names a broader role that load balancing is only one part of. Running on the same instance is an implementation detail, not proof the concepts are identical.

mcqs.question: A school network blocks access to certain categories of websites for every device on its network, enforced at one central point rather than per device. What kind of proxy is this?
options: A reverse proxy, since it's protecting the servers being accessed
A forward proxy configured for content filtering, since it controls outbound access on behalf of many clients from one central point
An API gateway, since it enforces policy
A load balancer, since it distributes traffic across multiple paths
mcqs.explanation: This is the forward-proxy pattern applied to policy enforcement instead of anonymity or caching — one gateway mediates outbound traffic for many clients. It isn't protecting the destination servers (that would be reverse-proxy territory), it isn't managing API-level identity or rate limits, and it isn't distributing load across backends.

mcqs.question: A backend logs the first IP address in the X-Forwarded-For header as "the real client IP." Why is this unsafe?
options: X-Forwarded-For is encrypted and cannot be read by the backend at all
Any client can set X-Forwarded-For to an arbitrary value before the request reaches the trusted proxy, so the first entry in the chain is an unverified claim, not a verified fact
X-Forwarded-For only ever contains exactly one IP address, so there is no 'first' to worry about
This is actually the correct and safe way to extract the client IP
mcqs.explanation: A malicious client can prepend any value it wants to X-Forwarded-For before the request ever reaches your trusted infrastructure, so trusting the first (client-supplied) entry is trivially spoofable. The safe pattern is trusting only the entry appended by your own known, trusted proxy. The header is plaintext, not encrypted, and can contain multiple comma-separated IPs, not just one.
